items.question: Distinguish between constitutional, statutory and executive bodies with suitable examples, and explain why non-constitutional bodies have become indispensable to modern governance in India.
items.modelAnswer:
Indian governance rests on a layered institutional architecture in which bodies differ fundamentally by their **source of authority**. A **constitutional body** is expressly created by the Constitution — such as the **Election Commission (Art 324)**, the **CAG (Art 148)**, the **UPSC (Art 315)** and the **Finance Commission (Art 280)** — and enjoys the highest protection, since altering it needs a constitutional amendment. A **statutory body** owes its existence to an **ordinary Act of Parliament or a State Legislature** — for example the **NHRC (1993)**, **CVC (2003)**, **SEBI (1992)**, **NGT (2010)**, **Lokpal (2013)** and **CIC (2005)**. An **executive (non-statutory) body** is set up by a mere **government resolution**, as with the **NITI Aayog (2015)** and the **Law Commission of India (1955)**.

Non-constitutional bodies have grown indispensable for several reasons. First, they provide **flexibility** — a regulator or commission can be created, restructured or wound up to meet changing needs without the rigidity of amending the Constitution. Second, they supply **sectoral expertise**: technical regulators like the **RBI, SEBI, TRAI, IRDAI and CCI** bring domain knowledge that a general legislature or executive cannot. Third, they enable **effective policy implementation and rights protection** — the NHRC safeguards human rights, the NGT delivers speedy environmental justice, and the Lokpal targets high-level corruption. In Andhra Pradesh, the **Lokayukta (1983 Act)** illustrates how States pioneered such institutions.

However, their statutory status makes them vulnerable to **executive encroachment** — seen in debates over CBI autonomy, the **RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019** diluting CIC independence, and the Supreme Court's **2025 verdict striking down parts of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021**. Strengthening their independence in appointments, tenure and funding is therefore essential so that flexibility does not come at the cost of accountability.
keyPoints: Constitutional (ECI, CAG, UPSC, Finance Commission) vs statutory (NHRC, SEBI, NGT, Lokpal, CIC) vs executive (NITI Aayog, Law Commission).
Source of authority is the key test — Constitution vs Act vs government resolution.
Non-constitutional bodies give flexibility, sectoral expertise and implementation capacity.
Regulators (RBI, SEBI, TRAI, IRDAI, CCI) supply technical domain expertise.
Independence concerns: CBI autonomy, RTI Amendment 2019, 2025 SC verdict on Tribunals Reforms Act 2021.
AP example: Lokayukta under the AP Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta Act, 1983.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Non-Constitutional Bodies; RTI Act 2005 & 2019; SC Tribunals Reforms judgment 2025

items.question: Regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies combine legislative, executive and judicial functions. Examine their role in India and the challenges to their independence.
items.modelAnswer:
As the state shifted from a **command-and-control** model to that of a **facilitator**, India built a set of **regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies** that concentrate three functions once kept separate — they **make rules** (legislative), **enforce and supervise** (executive) and **adjudicate disputes and impose penalties** (judicial). **SEBI** governs the securities market, the **RBI** banking and monetary policy, **TRAI** telecom, **IRDAI** insurance, **PFRDA** pensions and the **CCI** competition; quasi-judicial tribunals such as the **NGT** and the **Central Administrative Tribunal** (under **Articles 323A/323B**, added by the 42nd Amendment) deliver specialised, speedy justice.

Their **value** lies in expertise, quick disposal, investor and consumer confidence, and relief to overburdened courts — the NGT's binding environmental orders and SEBI's investor-protection powers are cases in point. Yet several **challenges** threaten their credibility. **Independence in appointments, tenure and funding** is fragile because most are statutory, not constitutional — the government is often the **largest litigant** before tribunals it also staffs and funds. The Supreme Court underscored this in its **November 2025 judgment striking down key provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021**, directing a **National Tribunal Commission**. Other concerns include the **concentration of powers** raising separation-of-powers questions, **regulatory capture**, overlapping jurisdictions, delays from vacancies, and limited accountability of expert members.

The way forward is an **arm's-length design** — independent, transparent selection committees, secure tenure and financial autonomy, clear appellate paths to constitutional courts, and periodic performance review — so that these bodies remain both **expert and independent** pillars of good governance.
keyPoints: Regulators/quasi-judicial bodies fuse legislative (rule-making), executive (supervision) and judicial (adjudication) roles.
Examples: SEBI, RBI, TRAI, IRDAI, PFRDA, CCI; tribunals NGT and CAT under Art 323A/323B.
Value: expertise, speedy justice, investor/consumer confidence, relief to courts.
Challenge: fragile independence in appointments, tenure and funding; government is largest litigant.
2025 Supreme Court verdict on Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 and call for a National Tribunal Commission.
Reforms: independent selection, secure tenure, financial autonomy, clear appeals, performance review.
items.source: Constitution Arts 323A/323B; NGT Act 2010; regulator Acts; SC Tribunals Reforms judgment 2025
